list.listitem: There is no evidence to support ovarian cancer screening by ultrasound or CA-125 in average risk women or in higher risk women, with no randomized trials finding lower disease-specific or overall mortality.. B

Symptoms that most increased the likelihood of ovarian cancer when present were abdominal mass (LR+ 30); abdominal distension or increased girth (LR+ 16); abdominal or pelvic pain (LR+ 10.4) or bloating (LR+ 9.3); loss of appetite (LR+ 9.2); and family history of ovarian cancer (LR+ 7.5). Women with persisent symptoms should be evaluated with a CA-125 level and pelvic ultrasound. C
The ultrasound characteristics of a pelvic mass are the most important independent predictors of malignancy in premenopausal women. B

Characteristics that increase the likelihood of malignancy in patients with pelvic mass include prepubescent or postmenopausal age, complex or solid appearance of mass on ultrasound, known non-gynecologic cancer, or ascites. C

Ovarian cysts in postmenopausal women should be assessed promptly using CA-125 and transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS). Use of human epididymis protein 4 (HE4) or a validated risk score such as the Risk of Ovarian Malignancy Algorithm (ROMA) increases specificity for ovarian cancer. C

background.definition: Pathologic mass of the adnexa (ovaries, fallopian tubes, vessels, ligaments or connective tissues), uterus, bowel, or retroperitoneal structures; may be metastatic from other sites.

list.listitem: Approximately 289,000 women are hospitalized annually in the United States due to an ovarian neoplasm.
In a low-dose unenhanced CT screening cohort of 2,751 women aged 50 years and older with initial negative adnexal findings, four cases of ovarian cancer developed during a 15- to 44-month interval.
The overall risk of malignancy in premenopausal women with an adnexal mass on ultrasound is 6% to 11%; in post-menopausal women the risk is 29% to 35%.

The prevalence of adnexal lesions on ultrasound exam in asymptomatic women ages 25 to 40 years is 7.8%. Most of these were ovarian cysts; four out of five cysts will resolve spontaneously within 3 months.
In the screening study presented above, 4.1% of the 118 women had an indeterminate adnexal mass identified; subsequent work-up of 80 cases revealed no ovarian cancers.
Ovarian cancer is the fifth leading cause of cancer-related deaths.
Malignancy (e.g., ovarian, metastatic)
Benign neoplasm (ovarian, leiomyoma, endometrioma)
Physiologic/functional cysts
Infectious
Pregnancy-related
Malignant ovarian neoplasms originate from epithelial cells, germ cells, sex cord stromal and mixed type cells.
Metastatic masses are usually of gastrointestinal (GI) or breast origin.
Leiomyomata are benign growths of uterine smooth muscle.
Physiologic/functional cysts arise from anovulatory ovarian follicles that continue to grow or a corpus luteum that fails to regress.
Infectious causes include pyosalpinx or hydrosalpinx, tubo-ovarian abscesses, or bowel-related abscesses.
Pregnancy-related masses can be ectopic pregnancy, theca lutein cysts or corpus luteum of pregnancy.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Family history of breast or ovarian CA
Family history of BRCA 1 or 2 genes

list.listitem: The USPSTF (2018) and the American College of Physicians (ACP) recommend against routine screening for ovarian cancer.

The USPSTF (2017) concludes that the current evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of performing screening pelvic examinations in asymptomatic women for the early detection and treatment of a range of gynecologic conditions. This statement does not apply to specific disorders for which the USPSTF already recommends screening (i.e., screening for cervical cancer with a Papanicolaou [“Pap”] smear, screening for gonorrhea and chlamydia).
The American College of Physicians recommends against performing screening pelvic examinations in asymptomatic, non-pregnant adult women.
There is no evidence that any screening test, including CA-125, ultrasound, or pelvic examination, can reduce mortality from ovarian cancer.
Prophylactic oophorectomy should be offered to women with mutations of BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes and women with two or more first-degree relatives with ovarian cancer at a relevant time in their lives.
There is no evidence that any screening test, including CA-125, ultrasound, or pelvic examination, can reduce mortality from ovarian cancer.

The USPSTF (2018), American College of Radiology (ACR 2018), and the ACP recommend against routine screening for ovarian cancer in asymptomatic women (D recommendation). Due to the low prevalence of ovarian cancer and the invasive nature of diagnostic testing after positive screening tests, there is fair evidence that screening will likely lead to important harms that outweigh the potential benefits.

The USPSTF (2017) concludes that the current evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of performing screening pelvic examinations in asymptomatic women for the early detection and treatment of a range of gynecologic conditions. This statement does not apply to specific disorders for which the USPSTF already recommends screening (i.e., screening for cervical cancer with a Papanicolaou [“Pap”] smear, screening for gonorrhea and chlamydia).
The American College of Physicians recommends against performing screening pelvic examinations in asymptomatic, non-pregnant adult women.

Ovarian cancer mortality does not significantly differ between screened women and those with no screening or in usual care. Screening harms included surgery (with major surgical complications) in women found to not have cancer. Further research is needed to identify effective approaches for reducing ovarian cancer incidence and mortality.

RCTs confirmed that annual screening for ovarian cancer with CA-125 and transvaginal ultrasound does not reduce ovarian cancer-specific mortality or all-cause mortality in otherwise healthy women at average risk for ovarian cancer; screening may cause unnecessary harm. The UKCTOCS study combining a clinical risk assessment with a CA-125 with the cutoff for abnormal tailored to the patient failed to find a reduction in ovarian cancer specific mortality.
Family history screening is helpful in identifying primary care patients at increased risk of ovarian cancer.
Screening does not appear to raise anxiety but psychological morbidity is elevated by more intense repeat testing following abnormal annual screens.

Some societies recommend consideration of screening with pelvic ultrasound and CA-125 in women at high risk, although its use in this setting is not supported by data demonstrating a mortality benefit.
Serum CRP levels may serve as an indicator of ovarian cancer risk. Further studies are needed to elucidate the role of CRP in the pathophysiology of ovarian cancer.
Screening for and treatment of cervicitis prevents many infectious causes of pelvic mass.

Use of oral contraceptives (OCs) decreases the relative risk of ovarian cancer. In one meta-analysis, the odds ratio was 0.73 (95% CI, 0.66-0.81) for ever use. A dose-response effect was also seen, with a reduction of more than 50% among women who used OCs for 10 years or more.

Women with a strong family history of ovarian, breast, or colon cancer may have hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome (BRCA mutation) or hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome), and these women are at increased risk of developing ovarian cancer. Women with these conditions should be referred for formal genetic counseling to better assess their cancer risk, including their risk of ovarian cancer. If appropriate, these women may be offered additional testing for early detection of ovarian cancer. This includes use of transvaginal ultrasonography and tumor markers (such as cancer antigen 125), alone or in combination.

Clinical genetic testing for gene mutations allows more precise identification of those women who are at an increased risk of inherited breast cancer and ovarian cancer. For these individuals, screening and prevention strategies can be instituted to reduce risk.
Prophylactic oophorectomy should be offered to women with mutations of BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes at a relevant time in their lives.
Bilateral salpingectomy for ovarian cancer prevention was safe and feasible and has the potential to be a cost-effective and cost-saving strategy across the population of patients at increased risk.
Risk-reducing early salpingectomy and delayed oophorectomy may be a promising alternative to mitigate quality of life-related risks of risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy.
Women with two or more first-degree relatives with ovarian cancer should be offered prophylactic oophorectomy after completing childbearing or at age 35 years.
According to a Cochrane review, green tea consumption for cancer prevention of any type has insufficient and conflicting evidence for any firm recommendations.

Symptoms that most increased the likelihood of ovarian cancer when present were abdominal mass (LR+ 30); abdominal distension or increased girth (LR+ 16); abdominal or pelvic pain (LR+ 10.4) or bloating (LR+ 9.3); loss of appetite (LR+ 9.2); and family history of ovarian cancer (LR+ 7.5). Women with persisent symptoms should be strongly considered for further evaluation with CA-125 and pelvic ultrasound. C
The ultrasound characteristics of a pelvic mass are the most important independent predictors of malignancy in premenopausal women. C
Ovarian cysts in postmenopausal women should be promptly assessed using CA-125 and transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS). C
Postmenopausal women with ovarian inclusion cysts identified on ultrasound, however, are not at increased risk of ovarian or breast cancer. C

list.listitem: Age is an important factor in the evaluation; prepubescent or postmenopausal women with pelvic mass are more likely to have malignancy.
Family history of ovarian or breast cancer, or BRCA1 or 2 gene mutations, increase risk for malignancy.

A systematic review found the symptoms that most increased the likelihood of ovarian cancer, when present, were abdominal mass (positive likelihood ratio [LR+] 30); abdominal distension or increased girth (LR+ 16); abdominal or pelvic pain (LR+ 10.4) or bloating (LR+ 9.3); loss of appetite (LR+ 9.2); and family history of ovarian cancer (LR+ 7.5). However, no combination of symptoms was useful as a screening tool in a low-prevalence population.
A positive pregnancy test should suggest ectopic pregnancy or corpus luteum or theca lutein cyst.
Fever, abdominal pain, or pelvic pain suggests abscess.
Menstrual irregularity or dysmenorrhea suggests uterine-related mass or hormone-producing mass.
Despite low sensitivity of bimanual exam in screening for adnexal masses (45%), the sensitivity for detecting pelvic malignancies is somewhat higher (72%).

TVUS of the pelvis with Doppler color flow imaging for evaluation of size, consistency/characterization, origin of mass, vascularity and ancillary features (ascites, metastases) is the preferred initial imaging study. It is accurate for evaluation of suspected abscess as well as suspected malignancy.
The ultrasound characteristics of a pelvic mass are the most important independent predictors of malignancy in premenopausal women.

The American College of Radiology (ACR, 2018) recommend either TVUS, ultrasound duplex doppler or the pelvis or transabdominal pelvic ultrasound as usually appropriate in evaluating pre- or postmenopausal women witth suspected pelvic mass who are asymptomatic.
Postmenopausal women with ovarian cysts should be evaluated with a CA-125 in addition to aTVUS.

In a large UK ovarian cancer screening trial with 48,230 subjects, 2.5% of women had ovarian inclusion cysts identified at baseline. After 6 years of follow-up, there was no difference between observed versus expected incidence rates for ovarian or breast cancers among these women.

In one study, women with an adnexal mass having complex or solid morphology and a serum CA-125 value >35 units/mL were at high risk of malignancy (positive predictive value 84.7% and negative predictive value 92.4%). In this study, 77.3% of women with stage I and II ovarian cancer were correctly identified as were 98.6% of women with stage III and stage IV ovarian cancer.

A model to predict the risk of malignancy in adnexal masses using ultrasound features including ascites, tumor morphology and degree of vascularity has been validated through linkage to histopathologic diagnosis.

The IOTA (International Ovarian Tumor Analysis) ultrasound rules are predictive models to estimate the risk of malignancy in an ovarian mass based on ultrasound features. The Simple Rules model is used for patients undergoing surgery and is available online. The ADNEX model, which uses 3 clinical and 6 ultrasound predictors, estimates the probability/risk that an adnexal tumor is benign, borderline, early-stage malignant (stage I), late-stage malignant (stage II-IV), or metastatic. ADNEX is also available online at the same site. The Simple Rules and the ADNEX model have high sensitivity (92% and 96.5%, respectively) and specificity (96% and 71.3%, respectively) using a cut-off of 10% to predict malignancy.

The Risk of Malignancy Index or RMI is another scoring system using four ultrasound features, menopausal status, and CA-125. RMI is calculated as U x M x CA-125 where U is the ultrasound score (multilocular cysts, solid areas, metastases, ascites, bilateral lesions) with score of 0 if none are present, 1 if one is present, and 3 if 2 to 5 are present; M is menopausal status where score is 1 if premenopausal and score is 3 if postmenopausal (defined as no menses for >1 year or age >50 with hysterectomy).

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies found the ADNEX had a better diagnostic ability than the RMI. The sensitivity and specificity for the ADNEX combined with CA125 were 0.93 (95% CI 0.90 to 0.96) and 0.77 (95% CI 0.71 to 0.81) and for RMI combined with CA 125 they were 0.61 (95% CI 0.56 to 0.67) and 0.92 (95% CI 0.89 to 0.94).

The addition of contrast-enhanced ultrasound to RMI can improve diagnosis of an adnexal mass when the RMI score is in the gray zone. An overall sensitivity of 85.7% and a specificity of 92.0% is achieved by this sequential approach.

In a population of 472 women presenting with adnexal mass to a variety of health providers, 81% were ultimately diagnosed with benign disease. Use of the Risk of Ovarian Malignancy Algorithm (ROMA which includes the biomarkers CA-125 and HE4) had 92.3% sensitivity for post-menopausal women and 100% sensitivity for premenopausal women for prediction of ovarian cancer; specificity was 74.2% and 74.9% respectively.

In a case series of women undergoing surgery for a pelvic mass, ROMA had better diagnostic performance for post-menopausal women than for pre-menopausal women (area under the curve [AUC] of 0.92 vs. 0.77). The AUCs for HE4 alone, however, were similarly high and better than CA-125 alone. One additional study found ROMA a better predictor of epithelial ovarian cancer than the Risk of Malignancy Index (established using CA-125, imaging score, and menopausal status).

Another transvaginal ultrasound-based prediction model performed better than ROMA for predicting malignancy among 360 women with a known pelvic mass who were scheduled for surgery. Malignancy was diagnosed in 144 of these women. The ultrasound model had a better overall test performance compared to ROMA with an AUC of 0.95 vs. 0.89 for ROMA. Variables in the ultrasound model included age, presence of ascites, the presence of blood flow within a papillary projection, maximal diameter of the solid component, irregular internal cyst walls, and the presence of acoustic shadows.

In a study of 200 female participants with pelvic masses who were scheduled to undergo biopsy or surgical excision, of whom 43% were diagnosed with a malignancy, a combination of 8 genes and 4 serum biomarkers had an AUC of 95.1% (95% CI 92.0% - 98.2%) and included 98.9% (96.7% - 100%) of patients with stage III-IV epithelial ovarian cancer. This combination requires validation in a larger patient population before its routine use in clinical practice.

CA-125 elevations are more predictive of malignancy in postmenopausal than in premenopausal women, but normal levels do not preclude malignancy in either group. Women over 50 years of age should be offered CA-125 testing if they have one or more symptoms of ovarian cancer including abdominal distention/bloating, fullness/loss of appetite, abdominal or pelvic pain, urinary frequency or urgency. Consider CA-125 testing for women over 50 who have weight loss or fatigue, change in bowel habits. If CA-125 is elevated (>35 units/ml), order pelvic and abdominal ultrasound within two weeks of CA-125 result. If the CA-125 is normal, or elevated but with normal ultrasound, patient should be reassessed in one month for persistent symptoms.

Human epididymis protein 4 (HE4) may be more useful than CA-125 in determining whether an ovarian mass is malignant. In a systematic review of 13 studies, the overall positive and negative likelihood ratios for HE4 were 13.0 (95% CI, 8.2-20.7) and 0.23 (95% CI, 0.19-0.28). For CA-125 they were 4.2 (95% CI, 3.1-5.6) and 0.27 (95% CI, 0.23-0.31).

Napsin A is an extremely sensitive (100%) marker of ovarian clear cell carcinomas and exhibits very high specificity (100%) in distinguishing clear cell carcinomas from high-grade serous carcinomas and serous borderline tumors and 90% specificity in discriminating clear cell carcinomas from endometrioid carcinomas.
Order serum beta-HCG to rule-out pregnancy-related causes of pelvic mass in women of childbearing age.
Order CBC to evaluate for possible infectious causes.
Order cervical cultures for gonorrhea and chlamydia.
Other tumor markers include alpha fetoprotein (AFP) for endodermal sinus tumors, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) for dysgerminomas, and beta-hCG for non-gestational carcinomas.
Women <40 years of age with symptoms of of ovarian cancer should be offered AFP, beta-hCG and CA-125 to identify women who may not have epithelial-type ovarian cancer.
Multiplexed gene expression analysis of cells captured from peripheral blood with or without serum biomarker levels, accurately detects malignancy in women with a pelvic mass.
The role of specific inflammatory cytokines biomarker pathways in cancer etiology is under investigation.

A combination of 8 genes and 4 serum biomarkers for use as testing to predict malignancy in a pelvic mass in females could be accurate enough for use in practice. This combination needs to be validated in a larger patient population before its routine use in clinical practice.

ACR (2018) recommends computed tomography (CT) abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) pelvis without and with IV contrast as the most appropriate follow-up test for women with suspected malignancy of an adnexal mass on ultrasound.
MRI has a reasonably high sensitivity (92%) for ruling out ovarian cancer (malignant or borderline; negative likelihood ratio 0.09).
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE, 2012) recommend MRI for further characterization of an indeterminate adnexal mass on ultrasound.

Most ovarian lesions contain solid and cystic parts which make the malignant and benign lesions look similar on imaging modalities. Using real-time sonoelastography as an adjunct to other imaging modalities may improve the differentiation of malignant ovarian lesions from benign lesions. Malignant ovarian lesions have softer tissue property than benign lesions and cystic lesions in terms of elastogram characteristics.
Diffusion-weighted MRI by using quantitative kurtosis variables might be of future help in clinical practice, especially in patients with contraindication to contrast media application.

Ovarian-Adnexal Reporting and Data System (O-RADS) scoring ultrasound and O–RADS MRI both have high sensitivity for ovarian and adnexal malignancy. O–RADS MRI also has high specificity based on 26 studies comprising 9520 patients in a systematic review and meta-analysis.

The O-RADS US risk stratification and management system enabled accurate distinction of benign from malignant ovarian and adnexal lesions. Adding acoustic shadowing as a benign finding improved its diagnostic performance.The highest risk of cancer was in isolated non-classic lesions with blood flow in women older than 60 years.
FDG-PET/CT scanning may be valuable in increasing the diagnostic accuracy including assessment of regional lymph nodes and distant metastases.
As a supplementary imaging technology, spectral CT (dual energy CT) can assist in differentiating benign and malignant ovarian tumors.
Final diagnosis of ovarian neoplasm is made by pathologic examination of surgically-removed tissue.
Obtain a menstrual and sexual history. The physical examination should include an abdominal and pelvic bimanual exam.

In premenopausal women, the work-up should include a complete blood count (CBC), beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG), cervical cultures for gonorrhea and chlamydia, Pap smear, and transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS).
In postmenopausal women, the work-up should include a CBC, Pap smear, CA-125 and TVUS, with consideration of HE4.
Interpret test results using a validated score such as the Risk of Malignancy Index, Risk of Ovarian Malignancy Algorithm, the Simple Rules model (online) or the ADNEX model (online).
A NICE statement (2012) recommends referral for patients whose Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI) is >250.
